params.question: Which cell is described as the key orchestrating cell in wound healing, responsible for clearing dead tissue and releasing the growth factors that drive the proliferative phase?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neutrophils are the first white blood cells to arrive during inflammation, but their role is to kill bacteria and clear debris. They do not orchestrate the transition to proliferation.
Correct. Macrophages take over from neutrophils, continue removing dead tissue, and release the growth factors that stimulate fibroblasts and angiogenesis in the proliferative phase.
Fibroblasts are the collagen-producing cells of the proliferative phase. They respond to growth factors released by macrophages rather than orchestrating the healing cascade.
Myofibroblasts are specialised contractile cells responsible for wound contraction during proliferation, not for orchestrating the overall healing programme.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the inflammatory phase: neutrophils arrive first to kill bacteria, but macrophages then take over as the key orchestrating cell, releasing the growth factors that drive the entire proliferative phase.

Well done. Macrophages are central to wound healing — they bridge the inflammatory and proliferative phases by clearing debris and releasing growth factors that recruit fibroblasts and drive angiogenesis.

interactions.label: In the opening case, diabetes, malnutrition, and smoking together delay healing

params.question: In the opening case, diabetes, malnutrition, and smoking together delay healing in the sixty-two-year-old patient. Which analysis of how each factor impairs healing is most accurate?

answers.text: Diabetes impairs leucocyte function, malnutrition removes collagen substrates, and smoking causes tissue hypoxia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Diabetes impairs leucocyte function and causes microvascular disease; malnutrition deprives the body of protein, vitamin C, and zinc needed for collagen synthesis; smoking adds vasoconstriction and tissue hypoxia.

answers.text: Diabetes causes vasoconstriction, malnutrition impairs leucocyte function, and smoking destroys collagen cross-links

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This misattributes the mechanisms. Vasoconstriction is caused by smoking, not diabetes. Malnutrition removes collagen substrates (protein, vitamin C, zinc); it does not impair leucocyte function.

answers.text: All three factors primarily impair the remodelling phase of wound healing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These factors affect multiple phases — diabetes blunts inflammation, malnutrition impairs proliferative collagen synthesis, and smoking reduces oxygen delivery throughout. They are not confined to remodelling.

answers.text: These are non-modifiable factors that cannot be addressed as part of surgical management

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration explicitly states that most systemic factors are modifiable. Optimising glycaemic control, correcting malnutrition, and stopping smoking are genuine surgical treatments.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the systemic factors: diabetes impairs leucocyte function and causes microvascular disease; malnutrition removes protein, vitamin C, and zinc for collagen; smoking causes vasoconstriction and tissue hypoxia. Crucially, most are modifiable.

Excellent. Understanding which mechanism each systemic factor disrupts helps you prioritise pre-operative optimisation — glycaemic control for leucocyte function, nutritional support for collagen synthesis, and smoking cessation for tissue oxygenation.

params.question: During an elective cholecystectomy, the biliary tract is entered under controlled conditions without spillage. Under the CDC wound classification, this surgical wound belongs to which class?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Class I (clean) applies only when no hollow viscus is entered. A cholecystectomy enters the biliary tract, so it cannot be classified as clean regardless of how controlled the procedure is.
Correct. Class II applies when a hollow viscus is entered under controlled conditions without significant spillage, carrying a surgical-site infection risk of roughly three to five per cent.
Class III applies to fresh traumatic wounds or procedures with gross spillage from a hollow viscus — not a controlled elective entry without spillage.
Class IV requires established infection or devitalised tissue at the operative site. An elective cholecystectomy without these findings does not meet this classification.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the key distinction: Class I = no hollow viscus entered; Class II = hollow viscus entered under controlled conditions. Cholecystectomy enters the biliary tract, making it Class II with a three-to-five per cent infection risk.
Well done. Recognising that any controlled entry into a hollow viscus places the wound in Class II is essential for predicting infection risk and guiding antibiotic and closure decisions.

params.question: A young man presents with a contaminated laceration on the forearm sustained two hours ago. After controlling haemorrhage, what is the single most important next step?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antibiotics are adjuncts to wound management and should never substitute for mechanical cleaning and debridement. They follow irrigation and debridement in the management sequence.
Closing a contaminated wound without first cleaning it risks trapping bacteria inside. The principle is absolute: never close a wound you have not satisfied yourself is clean.

answers.text: Irrigate the wound copiously with normal saline

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Copious normal saline irrigation does more to reduce bacterial load than any other single measure. It must precede debridement, closure decisions, and adjunctive antibiotics.

answers.text: Apply a sterile dressing and arrange delayed primary closure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While delayed primary closure may ultimately be appropriate for a contaminated wound, dressing it without first irrigating and debriding leaves contaminants in place and increases infection risk.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the wound management sequence: after controlling haemorrhage, copious normal saline irrigation is the next step — this single measure does more to reduce bacterial load than anything else, and must precede debridement and closure.

Correct. Copious saline irrigation after haemorrhage control is the most effective single step for reducing bacterial load — always performed before debridement, closure decisions, and adjunctive antibiotics.
